blogs.title: The 0.3 mg Epinephrine Auto-Injector in Adults: Convenient, Fast, and Underdosing Your Patient
blogs.description: This post examines the persistent gap between guideline-recommended epinephrine dosing (0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg) and the widespread use of 0.3 mg auto-injectors in adults over 50 kg. Using the presented case—where the first two anaphylactic episodes were treated with 0.3 mg auto-injector doses before switching to 0.5 mg individually prepared doses—we explore the trade-offs between speed/hesitancy reduction and critical underdosing. We review recent evidence showing that patients receiving 0.3 mg require significantly more escalation of care, and discuss strategies to align clinical practice with weight-based dosing recommendations while preserving the benefits of auto-injector use in time-sensitive or low-frequency settings.

blogs.title: Corticosteroids for Anaphylaxis: A Ritual Whose Time Has Passed?
blogs.description: This post critically appraises the evolving evidence on corticosteroid use in anaphylaxis, once routinely recommended for biphasic reaction prevention. Using the presented case—where the patient received both prednisone and dexamethasone due to conflicting hospital protocols despite already developing recurrent anaphylaxis—we review the 2017 systematic review and subsequent studies showing no benefit and potential harm, including increased ICU/hospital admission rates. We discuss why clinical practice persists despite contemporary guideline shifts, the cognitive bias behind 'doing something' in uncertain situations, and what a modern, steroid-sparing anaphylaxis protocol should look like.

blogs.title: Biphasic, Multiphasic, Refractory: Making Sense of Complex Anaphylaxis Terminology and Management
blogs.description: This post dissects the definitions and clinical implications of biphasic, multiphasic, and refractory anaphylaxis—terms that are often used inconsistently in the literature and in practice. Using the presented case of four distinct anaphylactic episodes over 12 hours, we explore the challenge of differentiating true multiphasic reactions from sustained anaphylaxis with transient epinephrine response or ongoing allergen absorption. We then examine the two management approaches contemplated in the case—proactive continuous IV epinephrine infusion versus expectant observation—and discuss the deeply troubling absence of evidence-based or expert consensus guidance for multiphasic courses. We propose a framework for clinical decision-making when facing recurrent anaphylaxis and call for a national or international registry of these rare events.

blogs.title: When Anaphylaxis Won't Stop: Systemic Mastocytosis as a Hidden Driver of Severe, Recurrent Reactions
blogs.description: This post explores systemic mastocytosis as an important but underrecognized predisposing condition for severe and recurrent anaphylaxis. Using the presented case—where a woman in her 60s with multiphasic anaphylaxis was found to have elevated baseline tryptase, hepatomegaly, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and two WHO minor criteria for systemic mastocytosis—we discuss the pathophysiology of mast cell disorders, the diagnostic criteria (and why many patients fall short of formal diagnosis), and the clinical clues that should prompt suspicion. We review the relationship between mast cell mediator burden and anaphylaxis severity, and discuss how identifying underlying mastocytosis changes long-term management, including the need for perpetual trigger avoidance, epinephrine auto-injector carriage, and specialist follow-up.

blogs.title: Tryptase Timing in Anaphylaxis: The Missed Diagnostic Opportunity We Keep Repeating
blogs.description: This post addresses the critical importance of proper serial tryptase sampling in the workup of anaphylaxis, a step frequently missed or improperly timed in the acute setting. Using the presented case—where the first tryptase sample was drawn only during the third anaphylactic episode, well outside guideline-recommended intervals—we review the optimal sampling strategy (baseline, 1–2 hours after onset, and ≥24 hours after resolution), what tryptase kinetics can tell us about reaction severity and underlying mast cell disorders, and why the delta tryptase may matter more than any single value. We discuss practical barriers to obtaining timely samples in a busy ED, propose system-level solutions (standing order sets, nursing protocols), and emphasize how proper tryptase measurement can unmask systemic mastocytosis or other mast cell activation syndromes that alter long-term patient management.

blogs.title: Observation After Anaphylaxis: How Long Is Long Enough When the Evidence Won't Commit?
blogs.description: This post tackles the enduring clinical uncertainty around observation duration following anaphylaxis resolution. Using the presented case—where the patient's fourth anaphylactic episode occurred approximately 12 hours after initial presentation, well beyond some traditional 4–6 hour observation windows—we review the wide range of published biphasic reaction timings (up to 78 hours), the limitations of proposed risk predictors (delayed epinephrine, severity, multiple doses, prior biphasic reactions), and the UK 2021 three-tier risk-stratified approach. We discuss the tension between patient safety and resource stewardship, compare international guideline recommendations (WAO, Dutch NHG, UK Resuscitation Council), and propose a pragmatic, risk-adapted observation strategy that accounts for both clinical features and systems-level constraints.
